etymology: Scottish minister and theologian (1780-1847), leader of the Disruption of 1843 and first Moderator of the Free Church of Scotland.
biblical_def: Thomas Chalmers was the foremost Scottish churchman of his age, a preacher, theologian, and reformer whose ministry reshaped the Church of Scotland. Converted to a vital, evangelical faith in mid-career after years of nominal religion, he became a preacher of extraordinary power, best remembered for his sermon The Expulsive Power of a New Affection, which teaches that the human heart is not freed from the love of the world by mere prohibition, but only when a greater love — love for God in Christ — expels and replaces it. Chalmers gave himself to the care of the poor, pioneering a parish system of Christian charity in industrial Glasgow, and to the renewal of the church. He led the great Disruption of 1843, when more than four hundred ministers, for the sake of Christ's sole headship over His church and against state interference in the calling of pastors, walked out of the established Church of Scotland to form the Free Church, surrendering manses and stipends for conscience' sake. Chalmers stands in the dictionary as the leader of the Disruption and preacher of the expulsive power of a new affection, who taught that the love of Christ alone dethrones the love of the world, and that the crown rights of the Redeemer over His church are worth every earthly loss.
webster_summary: Scottish minister and theologian (1780-1847), leader of the 1843 Disruption that formed the Free Church of Scotland; preacher of The Expulsive Power of a New Affection, that only a greater love for Christ dethrones the love of the world.

corruption_summary: Chalmers's great insight corrects the moralism that fights worldliness by mere willpower and prohibition, recovering the truth that only a supreme love for Christ can expel the love of the world.
corruption_paragraphs: Willpower-moralism correction. Much religion tries to conquer sin by sheer prohibition, ordering the heart to stop loving the world without giving it anything better to love. Chalmers saw the futility: the heart cannot be emptied of one affection except by being filled with a stronger one. The dictionary holds his gospel insight — the love of the world is not driven out by law but expelled by a new and greater love for God in Christ. Sanctification is the redirection of the affections, not merely their suppression.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the crown rights of the Redeemer over His church. At the Disruption, Chalmers and four hundred ministers gave up their livings rather than submit the church's spiritual freedom to the state. The dictionary commends their costly stand: Christ alone is Head of His church, and His headship is worth the loss of manse, stipend, and security. The same conviction still calls the church to prize the lordship of Christ above every earthly comfort.

etymology: Scottish minister (1680-1754), "father of the Secession," defender of free grace in the Marrow controversy.
biblical_def: Ebenezer Erskine was a Scottish Presbyterian minister, remembered as the father of the Secession Church and a stalwart defender of the free offer of the gospel. He stood among the "Marrow Men," the ministers who upheld the doctrine of The Marrow of Modern Divinity when the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland condemned it — defending the free, unconditional offer of Christ to sinners against a creeping legalism that fenced grace behind preparatory qualifications. Erskine preached that Christ is freely given to all who hear, and that the warrant to believe rests not on anything in the sinner but on God's gracious offer. In 1733, protesting the imposition of unwanted ministers on congregations through the patronage system and the spiritual decline of the established church, he led the First Secession, forming the Associate Presbytery so that congregations might call their own pastors and the gospel be freely preached. Erskine stands in the dictionary as the father of the Secession and a Marrow man, who contended for the free offer of Christ against legalism and for the people's right, under Christ's headship, to a faithful and freely-chosen ministry of the Word.
webster_summary: Scottish minister (1680-1754), father of the Secession Church; a "Marrow Man" who defended the free, unconditional offer of Christ against legalism, and led the 1733 Secession over patronage and the church's decline.

corruption_summary: Erskine's stand defends the free offer of the gospel against legalism that hedges grace behind qualifications, and the spiritual freedom of the church against patronage imposed by the state.
corruption_paragraphs: Legalism correction. A subtle legalism creeps in wherever the gospel offer is fenced behind preparatory works, telling sinners they must first qualify before they may come to Christ. The Marrow Men, Erskine among them, recovered the free offer: Christ is held out to all who hear, and the warrant to believe is God's gracious invitation, not any worthiness in the sinner. The dictionary holds the free offer of the gospel — "whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely" (Rev 22:17) — against every scheme that makes grace conditional on the creature.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the spiritual freedom of the church under Christ. Erskine seceded rather than submit to patrons forcing unwanted ministers on unwilling congregations. The dictionary commends the conviction: the church is Christ's, and the preaching of His free gospel must not be shackled to the interests of the powerful. The right of God's people to a faithful ministry of the Word is part of the crown rights of the Redeemer.

etymology: Scottish minister and poet (1685-1752), brother of Ebenezer, Secession leader and author of Gospel Sonnets.
biblical_def: Ralph Erskine was a Scottish Presbyterian minister and sacred poet, the younger brother of Ebenezer Erskine and, with him, a leader of the Secession Church. Like his brother he was a Marrow Man, contending for the free offer of the gospel and the doctrines of grace against the legalism that troubled the church of his day. He is remembered above all for his Gospel Sonnets, or Spiritual Songs, a much-loved collection of devotional verse that sets forth the believer's union with Christ, the contest between law and grace, the marriage of the soul to the Savior, and the experience of faith in vivid and tender poetry. His preaching was searching and Christ-centered, pressing the riches of free grace upon the conscience. Joining his brother in the First Secession of 1733, Ralph gave his strength to the cause of a free and faithful gospel ministry. He stands in the dictionary as the poet of the Secession and a Marrow man, who sang the free grace of Christ in verse that fed the godly for generations, and who taught the church that the deepest doctrines of grace are not cold abstractions but the very music of the redeemed heart.
webster_summary: Scottish minister and sacred poet (1685-1752), brother of Ebenezer and Secession leader; a Marrow Man whose Gospel Sonnets set the free grace of Christ and the believer's union with Him in beloved devotional verse.

corruption_summary: Erskine's verse honors the recovery of free grace and union with Christ as the heart's true song, against both a legalism that chills the gospel and a sentimentalism that empties devotion of doctrine.
corruption_paragraphs: Doctrine-poetry divorce correction. Some imagine that careful doctrine and warm devotion belong to separate worlds, the one dry, the other vague. Erskine's Gospel Sonnets refute the divorce: here the most exact truths of free grace, union with Christ, and the believer's marriage to the Savior are set to tender, scriptural verse. The dictionary holds that sound doctrine is the substance of true devotion; the deepest theology, when tasted, becomes song, and the godly poet teaches even as he delights.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the experiential sweetness of union with Christ. Erskine sang, with the bride of the Song, "My beloved is mine, and I am his." The dictionary commends his witness: the believer's union with Christ is not a bare doctrine but a living marriage, the soul wedded to its Redeemer, dead to the law and bringing forth fruit unto God. Such truth is meant to be experienced and sung, not merely defined.

etymology: Scottish Covenanter (c.1583-1646), co-author of the National Covenant and a Scottish commissioner to the Westminster Assembly.
biblical_def: Alexander Henderson was, after John Knox, the most influential churchman in the history of the Scottish Reformation, a leader of the Covenanter movement and a chief architect of Presbyterian Scotland. Converted from a moderate, episcopally-inclined ministry to a fervent Presbyterian conviction, he became the foremost statesman of the Kirk. In 1638 he was a principal author of the National Covenant, the great bond by which the Scottish people swore to maintain the Reformed religion against the imposition of bishops and a foreign liturgy by the crown. As Moderator of the Glasgow Assembly that year, he led the abolition of episcopacy in Scotland. He was one of the Scottish commissioners to the Westminster Assembly, where he labored alongside the English divines in framing the Confession and Catechisms, and he had a leading hand in the Solemn League and Covenant of 1643. Henderson stands in the dictionary as the great Covenanter statesman, who gave his life to the cause of Christ's sole kingship over His church and the freedom of the Kirk from royal control, and whose labors helped shape the Reformed and Presbyterian heritage confessed at Westminster.
webster_summary: Scottish Covenanter (c.1583-1646), after Knox the most influential churchman of the Scottish Reformation; a principal author of the 1638 National Covenant and a Scottish commissioner to the Westminster Assembly.

corruption_summary: Henderson's labor honors the recovery of Christ's sole headship over His church and the right of the church to order its worship by God's Word, against the state's claim to govern the conscience and the worship of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Erastian correction. The crown of Henderson's day claimed authority to impose bishops and a liturgy on the Scottish church, subjecting the worship of God to the will of the state. The National Covenant answered with the crown rights of Christ: He alone is Head of His church, and her worship and government are to be ordered by His Word, not by royal decree. The dictionary holds the spiritual independence of the church under Christ against every Erastian claim that would make the magistrate lord of the conscience.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is covenanting faithfulness. The National Covenant was a solemn, public, corporate vow to maintain the true religion, in the pattern of Israel's covenant renewals (2 Chr 15; Neh 9). The dictionary commends, with sober historical discernment of its turbulent age, the seriousness with which the Covenanters bound themselves before God to the cause of His truth, counting fidelity to Christ's kingship worth every earthly risk.

etymology: Scottish Covenanter theologian (1613-1648), the youngest member of the Westminster Assembly, author of Aaron's Rod Blossoming.
biblical_def: George Gillespie was a Scottish Covenanter and theologian who, though he died at only thirty-five, became one of the most brilliant debaters and acutest minds of the Westminster Assembly, to which he came as a Scottish commissioner. Despite being the youngest divine present, he was reckoned among its ablest, and tradition tells of his decisive interventions in debate. His major work, Aaron's Rod Blossoming, is the classic Presbyterian argument against Erastianism — the view that the civil magistrate holds supreme authority over the church. Gillespie contended that Christ has appointed in His church a government distinct from the civil power, with its own officers and discipline, answerable to Him alone; the keys of the kingdom belong to the church, not to the state. He also wrote against unwarranted ceremonies in worship, defending the regulative principle that God alone may prescribe how He is to be worshiped. Gillespie stands in the dictionary as the youthful champion of Presbyterian church government and the spiritual independence of the church, who taught that Christ rules His church through her own appointed government, and that her discipline and worship are subject to His Word, not to the will of the magistrate.
webster_summary: Scottish Covenanter theologian (1613-1648), the youngest and one of the ablest Westminster divines; author of Aaron's Rod Blossoming, the classic argument against Erastianism for the spiritual independence of the church.

corruption_summary: Gillespie's argument defends the spiritual independence of the church against Erastianism, which subjects the church to the state, recovering the truth that Christ governs His church through her own appointed officers and discipline.
corruption_paragraphs: Erastian correction. Erastianism makes the civil magistrate the supreme governor of the church, subjecting her discipline and worship to the state. Gillespie's Aaron's Rod Blossoming answers that Christ has given the keys of the kingdom to His church, not to the magistrate (Matt 16:19; 18:17), and that her government is spiritual, distinct from the civil power, and answerable to Christ alone. The dictionary holds the spiritual independence of the church against every claim, ancient or modern, that would make the state lord over the things of God.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is also the regulative principle of worship, which Gillespie defended: God alone has the right to determine how He is to be worshiped, and the church may not impose ceremonies of human invention. The dictionary commends both his doctrines as expressions of one truth — the kingship of Christ over His church, who governs her worship and discipline by His Word, that He might have the preeminence in all things.

etymology: Scottish Covenanter minister (1622-1658), author of Christ Crucified and a noted commentary on the Revelation.
biblical_def: James Durham was a Scottish Covenanter minister and theologian of great spiritual depth, who in a short life produced some of the richest practical and expository writing of the Scottish church. His Christ Crucified, seventy-two sermons on Isaiah 53, is a profound and tender exposition of the suffering Servant and the heart of the atonement, long treasured by the godly. He wrote a substantial commentary on the book of the Revelation, an exposition of the Ten Commandments (The Law Unsealed), and a wise and weighty treatise Concerning Scandal, on the causes and healing of division in the church, born of his grief over the bitter splits among the Covenanters of his day. Durham combined doctrinal soundness with a rare pastoral tenderness and a deep concern for the unity and purity of the church. He stands in the dictionary as a Scottish expositor of the cross and a physician of the church's divisions, who set forth the crucified Christ with searching warmth, and who taught the church both to behold the depths of the Savior's suffering and to labor, in a divided age, for peace and holiness among the people of God.
webster_summary: Scottish Covenanter minister (1622-1658), author of Christ Crucified (on Isaiah 53), a commentary on Revelation, and a treatise Concerning Scandal; an expositor of the cross and a physician of the church's divisions.

corruption_summary: Durham's work honors the recovery of the cross as the heart of preaching and of patient labor for the church's unity and purity, against both a gospel emptied of the atonement and a contentiousness that needlessly divides the godly.
corruption_paragraphs: Cross-emptied correction. Where modern preaching often skirts the atonement, Durham's seventy-two sermons dwell at length on the wounded Servant of Isaiah 53, the chastisement of our peace upon Him. The dictionary holds with the apostle, "we preach Christ crucified" (1 Cor 1:23): the substitutionary suffering of Christ is the center of the gospel, and the church that turns from it has lost its message. Durham's example calls preachers back to the cross as the heart of their proclamation.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the careful handling of scandal and division. Durham, grieved by the splits among the Covenanters, wrote wisely on when division is warranted and how the godly may be reconciled. The dictionary commends his balance: the church must guard the truth, yet also labor to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, neither making peace by surrendering truth nor making division a habit of the contentious heart.

etymology: Scottish theologian and philosopher (1627-1653), author of The Common Principles of the Christian Religion, dead at twenty-six.
biblical_def: Hugh Binning was a Scottish minister of prodigious gifts, a philosopher and theologian who became a professor of philosophy at Glasgow in his teens and a parish minister soon after, yet died of consumption at only twenty-six, leaving behind writings of remarkable maturity and beauty. His works, gathered after his death, include The Common Principles of the Christian Religion (an exposition of the catechism), Fellowship with God (on the first epistle of John), and a moving treatise on Christian love, The Sinner's Sanctuary, and a plea for unity among the divided Scottish church, A Treatise of Christian Love. Binning's writing joins philosophical depth to a warm, contemplative piety, dwelling on the greatness of God, the wonder of communion with Him, and the supremacy of love. That so young a man wrote with such weight and sweetness has made him a marvel to later generations. Binning stands in the dictionary as a youthful genius of Scottish divinity, who in a brief life set forth the knowledge of God and fellowship with Him with rare depth and tenderness, and who pleaded with the divided church to be bound together in Christian love.
webster_summary: Scottish theologian and philosopher (1627-1653), a prodigy dead at twenty-six; author of The Common Principles of the Christian Religion and Fellowship with God, joining philosophical depth to warm piety and a plea for Christian love.

corruption_summary: Binning's writings honor the recovery of communion with God as the soul's chief good and of Christian love as the bond of the church, against a religion that knows much about God but little of Him, and contends without charity.
corruption_paragraphs: Knowledge-without-fellowship correction. It is possible to know much about God yet have little fellowship with Him. Binning's Fellowship with God presses past mere information to communion: the end of the gospel is that we have fellowship with the Father and with His Son (1 John 1:3). The dictionary holds that the knowledge of God is eternal life (John 17:3), not bare data about Him, and commends Binning's tender insistence that the soul was made to know and enjoy God Himself.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the supremacy of Christian love. Grieved by the divisions of the Scottish church, Binning pleaded for love as the bond that should unite the godly, with the apostle's verdict that the greatest of the graces is charity (1 Cor 13:13). The dictionary commends his plea: truth and love are not rivals, and a contending that has lost charity has lost its way. The church is to hold the truth in love, bound together by the love that is of God.

etymology: Scottish reformer and scholar (1545-1622), successor to John Knox as leader of the Kirk and champion of Presbyterian church government.
biblical_def: Andrew Melville was a Scottish scholar and churchman who, after the death of John Knox, became the leading figure of the Scottish Reformation and the chief architect of its Presbyterian polity. A brilliant classical and biblical scholar, he reformed the Scottish universities and trained a generation of ministers. His great cause was the government of the church: against the crown's effort to control the Kirk through bishops, Melville contended for a Presbyterian order in which Christ alone is King and Head of His church, governing her through assemblies of elders, not through prelates appointed by the state. In a famous confrontation he seized King James VI by the sleeve and called him "God's silly vassal," declaring that there were two kingdoms in Scotland — the kingdom of the commonwealth, in which the king was lord, and the kingdom of Christ the Church, in which the king was "not a king, nor a lord, nor a head, but a member." This was no privatizing of faith but a bold assertion of Christ's sole authority over His church, distinct from the civil power. Melville stands in the dictionary as the father of Scottish Presbyterianism, who championed the crown rights of Christ the King over His church against every claim of the state to rule the things of God.
webster_summary: Scottish reformer and scholar (1545-1622), successor to Knox and architect of Scottish Presbyterianism; who told King James VI that in the kingdom of Christ the Church he was "not a king... but a member," asserting Christ's sole headship over His church.

corruption_summary: Melville's "two kingdoms" asserts Christ's sole headship over His church against state control, and must not be confused with the modern radical two-kingdoms scheme that privatizes faith and silences the church before the world.
corruption_paragraphs: Erastian correction. Melville's life was given to resisting the crown's claim to govern the church through bishops. His "two kingdoms" meant that Christ alone is King and Head of His church, which the civil magistrate may not rule; in that kingdom the king is a member, not a lord. The dictionary holds this crown right of the Redeemer against every Erastian claim that the state may order the worship, government, or discipline of the church.

Radical-two-kingdoms confusion. Melville's doctrine must not be confused with the modern radical two-kingdoms (R2K) scheme, which uses the language of "two kingdoms" to privatize the faith, deny that Christ's lordship bears on public life, and silence the church's witness to the world. Melville asserted the opposite: not that Christ's reign is confined to a private sphere, but that His kingship over the church is supreme and beyond the magistrate's reach. The dictionary holds the crown rights of Christ over His church and His lordship over all of life together, against any scheme that would shrink His reign.
roots_summary: Scottish reformer and scholar (1545-1622), successor to Knox and architect of Scottish Presbyterianism; champion of Christ's sole headship over His church against royal control.

etymology: Scottish minister (1554-1631), powerful preacher at St Giles in Edinburgh and author of sermons on the Lord's Supper.
biblical_def: Robert Bruce was a Scottish minister of singular spiritual power, who left a noble and wealthy family to enter the ministry and became, after Knox and before Melville's full ascendancy, one of the most weighty preachers Scotland ever produced. Minister of St Giles in Edinburgh, he preached with such authority and presence that men said the Spirit of God was sensibly upon him; the godly traveled far to hear him. His most famous writings are his sermons on the Lord's Supper, The Mystery of the Lord's Supper, which set forth with reformed clarity the spiritual feeding of the believer upon the crucified Christ in the sacrament — not a bare memorial, nor a carnal presence, but a true partaking of Christ by faith through the working of the Spirit. Bruce suffered exile and opposition for his fidelity, particularly his refusal to flatter the king, yet remained immovable in his witness. He stands in the dictionary as a preacher of rare spiritual authority and an expositor of the Lord's Supper, who taught the church that in the sacrament the believer truly feeds by faith upon the whole Christ, and whose ministry bore the manifest weight of the presence of God.
webster_summary: Scottish minister (1554-1631), a preacher of rare spiritual power at St Giles in Edinburgh; author of The Mystery of the Lord's Supper, on the believer's true feeding upon Christ by faith in the sacrament.

corruption_summary: Bruce's teaching guards the Lord's Supper between two errors: a bare memorialism that empties the sacrament of Christ, and a carnal view that locates His body in the elements; he recovers the true spiritual feeding upon Christ by faith.
corruption_paragraphs: Bare-memorialism correction. Some reduce the Lord's Supper to a mere mental remembrance, a symbol empty of any real communion with Christ. Bruce, with the Reformed tradition, taught more: in the Supper the believer truly partakes of the body and blood of Christ — not carnally, but really and spiritually, by faith, through the Holy Spirit. The dictionary holds that the cup and bread are the communion of the blood and body of Christ (1 Cor 10:16); the sacrament conveys Christ to the believing soul, and is no empty sign.

Carnal-presence correction. The opposite error locates Christ's physical body in or under the elements, as though the bread became His flesh. Bruce held the Reformed middle way: Christ's body is in heaven, yet the believer, by the Spirit and through faith, is lifted to feed upon the whole Christ truly. The dictionary commends this teaching against both errors: "it is the spirit that quickeneth" (John 6:63), and the feeding is real but spiritual, received by faith, to the nourishing of the soul unto eternal life.

etymology: Scottish minister (1813-1843) of St Peter's, Dundee, known for personal holiness and a widely used Bible reading plan; dead at twenty-nine.
biblical_def: Robert Murray M'Cheyne was a Scottish minister of the Church of Scotland, pastor of St Peter's in Dundee, whose brief life of twenty-nine years left a lasting mark through the beauty of his personal holiness and the tenderness of his Christ-centered ministry. He labored amid a season of revival, preaching with affection and earnestness, and was so marked by communion with God that his very presence was said to convict. After his early death of typhus, his friend Andrew Bonar published the Memoir and Remains of Robert Murray M'Cheyne, which became one of the most influential devotional books in the English-speaking church, spreading his example of holiness far beyond his short life. M'Cheyne is also remembered for his Bible reading calendar, a plan that leads the believer through the whole Bible in a year, the New Testament and Psalms twice — still widely used today. His often-quoted conviction, that "the greatest need of my people is my personal holiness," captures his ministry. M'Cheyne stands in the dictionary as a pattern of pastoral holiness and a guide to the daily reading of Scripture, who taught the church that the minister's first work is to be a holy man, and that the daily, systematic reading of the whole Word is the food of the believing soul.

corruption_summary: M'Cheyne's life honors the recovery of personal holiness as the heart of ministry and the daily, systematic reading of the whole Bible, against a professionalized ministry that prizes skill over sanctity and a piecemeal reading that neglects the whole counsel of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Gifts-over-holiness correction. The modern church often prizes a minister's talent, charisma, and skill above his sanctity. M'Cheyne's conviction cuts the other way: "the greatest need of my people is my personal holiness." The dictionary holds with the apostle, "Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine" (1 Tim 4:16); the man is the message, and no eloquence can substitute for a holy life. M'Cheyne's example recalls every servant of God to the priority of personal godliness.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the daily, systematic reading of the whole Word. M'Cheyne's calendar leads the believer through all of Scripture in a year, refusing to leave any part neglected. The dictionary commends the discipline, fitting for a ministry like this one devoted to the reading of the Bible: the soul is fed by delighting in the law of the LORD and meditating in it day and night (Psa 1:2), and the whole counsel of God, read in order, is the believer's daily bread.
